[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and Gallup World Poll for East Asian countries (e.g., Japan, South Korea, China) during boom periods post-2000, matched with GDP growth rates — Directly tests whether subjective happiness trends diverge from GDP trajectories in collectivist contexts, controlling for time and cultural variables.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or survey-based studies on social comparison and perceived harmony loss in rapidly growing East Asian economies (e.g., using the Social Comparison Scale and Harmony Scale) — Provides causal evidence for the proposed mechanisms (increased social comparison and perceived loss of harmony) linking economic growth to reduced subjective well-being.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses or systematic reviews of subjective well-being and economic growth in collectivist versus individualist cultures (e.g., Easterlin paradox literature focused on East Asia) — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the divergence pattern is robust across studies and whether the proposed mechanisms are supported by prior findings.

C006.subject: subjective measures of happiness in collectivist cultures
C006.object: due to the integration of economic growth into societal values
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: subjective measures of happiness in collectivist cultures due to the integration of economic growth into societal values]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal World Values Survey (WVS) data for East Asian collectivist societies (e.g., Japan, South Korea, China) post-2000, analyzing the correlation between national GDP growth and self-reported life satisfaction or happiness scores. — Directly tests whether subjective happiness trends track GDP trends in the specified geographic and temporal scope, allowing for within-region comparison and control for confounds.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-cultural experimental studies comparing the weight individuals in collectivist vs. individualist cultures place on economic growth when evaluating personal happiness, using priming or vignette-based measures. — Tests the mechanism: whether integration of economic growth into societal values mediates the alignment, by isolating cultural value differences in the happiness–GDP link.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of anthropological and sociological literature on the concept of 'social progress' in East Asian collectivist societies, examining how economic growth is embedded in communal narratives of well-being (e.g., the 'Asian values' debate). — Provides theoretical grounding for the hypothesized value integration and helps interpret empirical findings within the cultural context.

C007.subject: subjective measures of happiness in high-GDP individualist cultures
C007.object: when controlling for income inequality and measuring social trust
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: subjective measures of happiness in high-GDP individualist cultures when controlling for income inequality and measuring social trust]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of World Values Survey (WVS) and European Social Survey (ESS) data for the specified countries, focusing on subjective well-being items, income inequality (Gini), and social trust indices post-2000. — These surveys provide repeated, cross-national measures of happiness, trust, and income inequality, enabling multilevel modeling to test whether subjective happiness diverges from GDP trends when controlling for these factors.

[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of the Easterlin Paradox literature using country-level panel data from OECD databases (GDP per capita, Gini coefficients) merged with Gallup World Poll happiness scores, with social trust as a moderator. — This directly tests the hypothesis by examining within-country and between-country variation in happiness relative to GDP, specifically isolating the role of income inequality and social trust in high-GDP individualist cultures.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical review of cultural individualism and its interaction with social capital, drawing on Putnam's 'Bowling Alone' and more recent work on declining social trust in affluent societies. — Provides a conceptual framework for why subjective happiness might decouple from GDP in individualist cultures when trust is low and inequality is high, helping to interpret empirical findings and identify causal mechanisms.

[PATH:empirical] Easterlin Paradox replication studies using individual-level panel data (e.g., German Socio-Economic Panel, British Household Panel Survey) — Provides micro-level evidence on the decoupling of happiness from income over time, addressing the hypothesis with within-country controls for inequality and cultural individualism.

[PATH:empirical] China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS) and China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) happiness modules (1989-2015) — Offers panel data on subjective happiness in China post-1978, a key case of rapid economic transition, enabling comparison of income inequality effects versus GDP growth effects over time.
